title: Mathurā
summary: The holy city where Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared in the prison of Kaṁsa.
body: Mathurā stands on the Yamunā and is one of the oldest holy cities in the region. It is remembered as the capital of the Yadu line. Kaṁsa ruled here when Kṛṣṇa appeared to Devakī and Vasudeva. The prison of that period is therefore central to the place's memory. After His childhood in Vraja, Kṛṣṇa returned to Mathurā. There He ended Kaṁsa's rule and restored His family's honour. The city links the story of birth with the story of return. Its position on the river made it a natural point of travel and pilgrimage. Nearby settlements and river crossings keep it tied to the wider Vraja landscape. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Vṛndāvana
summary: The forest of Vraja on the Yamunā where Kṛṣṇa spent his childhood with the cowherd boys and the cows.
body: Vṛndāvana is the principal sacred forest of Kṛṣṇa's childhood pastimes. Vraja tradition counts its sacred area as sixteen krośas across twelve principal forests. The landscape is imagined as groves, meadows, hills and the bank of the Yamunā. Cows, peacocks and birds belong to the daily setting of these stories. Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma are remembered here with the cowherd boys and the cattle. Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are honoured in the groves as the divine couple served by Their companions. When Rādhā once vanished, Kṛṣṇa searched the riverbank gardens for Her. The same forests later became the field of Caitanya's searching and discovery. Pilgrims come here to walk through the places where those pastimes are remembered. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Govardhana Hill
summary: The sacred hill in Vraja that Kṛṣṇa lifted to protect the residents from Indra's storm.
body: Govardhana Hill rises above the pastures of Vraja and supplies grass and water for the cattle. The cowherd community gathered around it in their daily work. It is honoured as more than an ordinary hill by those who remember Kṛṣṇa's pastimes there. The best-known event is Kṛṣṇa lifting it to shelter Vraja from a fierce storm. The residents took refuge beneath it with their cows and families. Indra's pride was checked, and the hill became a sign of protection. The event also taught Vraja to look to Kṛṣṇa rather than to celestial power. Parikrama paths around the hill keep that memory present in the landscape. Caves, springs and grazing grounds around it are visited as part of the same sacred circuit. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Madhuvana
summary: The forest on the Yamunā where young Dhruva practised austerity and saw the Lord.
body: Madhuvana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana and lies near the Yamunā. Its name is linked with Madhu, an old figure associated with the forest. The area was also connected with Maholī, an early settlement near Mathurā. Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma are remembered playing here with the cowherd boys. Honey from the forest became part of the childhood pastimes. Yaśodā's attempt to confirm Kṛṣṇa's whereabouts is recalled in connection with this place. Nārada directed Dhruva to this forest for austerity. Dhruva's steady practice there ended in the Lord's appearance before him. The forest thus holds both playful childhood memories and a story of severe devotion. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kurukṣetra
summary: The field where Kṛṣṇa gave His counsel to Arjuna between two armies.
body: Kurukṣetra is an ancient field of sacrifice and pilgrimage. It is best known as the site of the great conflict between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas. Kṛṣṇa served as Arjuna's charioteer when the armies stood facing one another. Arjuna's grief on the field became the occasion for Kṛṣṇa's counsel. That teaching concerns duty, knowledge, the self and devotion. The field therefore holds both the memory of war and the memory of instruction. Its sacred status draws visitors from many traditions. Pools and smaller sites around the field are linked with particular acts of pilgrimage. The place stands outside Vraja yet remains connected to Kṛṣṇa's wider story. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Tālavana
summary: The second forest on Vraja’s parikrama path, full of date-palm trees and known for a beautiful clear lake filled with blue lotuses.
body: Tālavana is the second forest on the Vraja parikrama path. It is known for date-palm trees and a clear lake filled with blue lotuses. The water of that lake is remembered as a place where wishes are fulfilled. In the New Vraja-dhāma setting, this forest is paired with Madhuvana. Balarāma's encounter with the donkey demon Dhenuka is recalled here. The gopas avoided the fruit associated with that disturbed place. Caitanya Mahāprabhu is remembered visiting Tālavana and honouring Balarāma. Bathing in Vetra-gaṅgā is part of the same local memory. The forest belongs to the western group of Vraja's sacred woods. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kumudavana
summary: Kumudavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, full of kumuda lotuses and known also as Kondaliyā, where Kṛṣṇa quarrelled with Śrīdāmā.
body: Kumudavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana. It is filled with kumuda lotuses and is also known as Koṇḍaliyā. Kṛṣṇa's quarrel with Śrīdāmā, Subala and the other gopas is remembered here. The Yamunā is said to have once wound through this forest. Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited the small grove on His travels through Vraja. Devotees who come with humility are remembered as finding success in their efforts. One night in Vaiśākha, Kṛṣṇa brought the gopīs here for a rāsa dance. The place is grouped with the forests west of the Yamunā. Its flowers and river setting give the forest its quiet character. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Bahulavana
summary: Bahulāvana is one of the twelve forests of Vraja, and it contains Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa in Bhauma Vṛndāvana.
body: Bahulavana is remembered here as bahulāvana is one of the twelve forests of Vraja, and it contains Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa in Bhauma Vṛndāvana. Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited, and the residents thought the sannyāsī was a fair-complexioned Śrī Kṛṣṇa as He smiled at them and chanted Kṛṣṇa's names. Within the forest are Saṅkarṣaṇa-kuṇḍa and Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa, and bathing in them during Caitra lets one see the forms of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa who eternally reside there. Vraja teachers suggest that the hills of New Vṛndāvana could be renamed after Govardhana. The site is grouped with places west of yamunā. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. title: Kāmyavana
summary: Kāmyavana is the fourth of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, known as the forest that fulfils all desires.
body: Kāmyavana is the fourth of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, known as the forest that fulfils all desires. The forest includes Kāma-sarovara and Kāmanā-kuṇḍa, and Kṛṣṇa played His flute from Candrasena Hill here, so that the girls of Vraja fainted. Kṛṣṇa and His friends once became so absorbed in play at Āṭora that twenty-four hours passed without their noticing. Vajranābha tradition links Kāmyavana with Kāmeśvara Mahādeva and Vṛndā-devī, two of the sixteen deities said to have been installed in Vraja. The site is grouped with places west of yamunā. title: Khadiravana
summary: Khadiravana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, named for its khadira (acacia) trees.
body: Khadiravana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, named for its khadira (acacia) trees. Merely visiting it can take one to Viṣṇuloka. Caitanya Mahāprabhu came here chanting in ecstatic love while His guide Kṛṣṇadāsa narrated Kṛṣṇa's pastimes there, and Lokanātha and Bhūgarbha Gosvāmīs performed bhajana here. The site is grouped with places west of yamunā. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Bhadravana
summary: Bhadravana is Lord Balarāma's favourite forest and is named after Him, Balabhadra, and it is one of the twelve forests of Vraja.
body: Bhadravana is Lord Balarāma's favourite forest and is named after Him, Balabhadra, and it is one of the twelve forests of Vraja. Rūpa Gosvāmī completed Lalita-mādhava on the bank of Bhadra-sarovara in this forest, and tradition says reading or hearing such traditions here is especially fitting. Sudāmā, one of Kṛṣṇa's gopa friends, prefers Bhadravana for frolicking with Kṛṣṇa. Vaikuṇṭha-pura, where Kṛṣṇa revealed the unlimited expanse of Vaikuṇṭha at His friends' request, lies in its southeastern corner. The site is grouped with places east of yamunā. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. title: Bhāṇḍīravana
summary: Bhāṇḍīravana is the forest named after the famous banyan Bhāṇḍīraka, also called Akṣaya-vaṭa, and it is listed among the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana.
body: Bhāṇḍīravana is the forest named after the famous banyan Bhāṇḍīraka, also called Akṣaya-vaṭa, and it is listed among the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana. Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were married here beneath the banyan, and the same name also belongs to a forest where Balarāma killed Pralambāsura, for which Indra gave Him the names Baladeva and Pralambaghna. Tradition recounts Rati-mañjarī bringing a picture of Kṛṣṇa to Rādhā while She sat in this forest, and Nārada Muni hearing two parrots debate the Vedānta teaching here. Hearing or reciting Vraja tradition of the wedding beneath this banyan is said to free one from the effects of past sins. The site is grouped with places east of yamunā. Figures linked with this place include Balarāma, Indra. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Bilvavana
summary: Bilvavana is one of the twelve great forests of Vṛndāvana, on the western side of the Yamunā.
body: Bilvavana is one of the twelve great forests of Vṛndāvana, on the western side of the Yamunā. The principal pastime described is that the goddess of fortune, Lakṣmī, performed austerities here hoping to be reborn as a gopī of Vraja, and she continues to do so invisibly, while a deity of her is worshipped here, which is why the forest is also called Śrīvana. This pastime shows the gopīs' unique standing as objects of Kṛṣṇa's favour, which Uddhava recognised during his visit to Vṛndāvana. The gopas also enjoyed the forest's fruits, using the hard-shelled ones as balls. Also spelled Baelvana. The site is grouped with places east of yamunā. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. Figures linked with this place include Uddhava. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Lohavana
summary: Lohavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, where the demon Loha once lived.
body: Lohavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, where the demon Loha once lived. After Kaṁsa was killed, his father-in-law Jarāsandha marched on Mathurā, camped at Lohavana, and surrounded the city. Kṛṣṇa devised a plan to destroy Jarāsandha's armies while sparing Jarāsandha himself. Tradition also mentions Ayore and Gauravāi on the perimeter, connected with Kṛṣṇa's return to Vṛndāvana, and alludes to the pastime of Kṛṣṇa as a boatman on the Yamunā. The spelling Lauhavana is also encountered as a variant of the same name. The site is grouped with places east of yamunā. title: Mahāvana
summary: Mahāvana is the first of the twelve main forests of Vṛndāvana, where Kṛṣṇa takes His birth.
body: Mahāvana is the first of the twelve main forests of Vṛndāvana, where Kṛṣṇa takes His birth. Once the cowherd men set up camp at Chaṭīkarā and formed a semicircular boundary with their carts, and Mahāvana was abandoned afterward. Vraja tradition also describes Kṛṣṇa revealing the entire universe within His body to the sage Durvāsā Muni, who had taken up residence near Rāval on the opposite side of Mahāvana from Gokula. The site is grouped with places east of yamunā. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Rādhā-kuṇḍa
summary: Rādhā-kuṇḍa is one of the most frequently discussed holy places in Vraja tradition, the lake of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's intimate pastimes.
body: Rādhā-kuṇḍa is a sacred lake in the Vraja landscape near Govardhana. It is honoured as the place where Rādhā and Her companions gather water for Kṛṣṇa. The lake is surrounded by groves that belong to the wider Rādhā-Nanda area. Its banks are associated with intimate service and confidential pastimes. Caitanya Mahāprabhu is remembered as discovering the site and revealing its importance. The nearby Śyāma-kuṇḍa is closely linked with the same circle of pastimes. Pilgrims bathe here and walk slowly around the water with devotion. The site is treated with great care because of its place in Vraja tradition. Its setting joins water, flowers and the memory of Rādhā's service. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Śyāma-kuṇḍa
summary: A sacred bathing pool in Vraja associated with Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
body: Śyāma-kuṇḍa is a sacred lake close to Rādhā-kuṇḍa. It is associated with Kṛṣṇa and the pastimes of the divine couple. The water and banks are remembered as part of the same confidential landscape. Caitanya Mahāprabhu's discovery of the two lakes links them in Vraja tradition. The site is approached with the same care given to Rādhā-kuṇḍa. Pilgrims come here to remember Kṛṣṇa's presence in the groves. Nearby paths connect the lake with Govardhana and the surrounding forests. Its name preserves the memory of Kṛṣṇa's dark complexion. The lake remains a focal point for those drawn to the rāgānugā mood. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Gokula
summary: A village in Vraja connected with Kṛṣṇa's family and pastimes.
body: Gokula is a settlement of Vraja closely linked with Kṛṣṇa's early childhood. It is remembered as a place of cattle, cowherd homes and family life. Nanda and Yaśodā are central to its domestic setting. Kṛṣṇa's first days after being brought across the Yamunā are connected with this area. The place recalls both protection and the ordinary work of a cowherd village. Later shrines in the region mark houses and scenes from those memories. Gokula is tied by path and story to Mahāvana and Nanda-grāma. Visitors come to see the setting of the Lord's earliest Vraja life. The name remains a simple reminder of cows, home and divine childhood. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Nanda-grāma
summary: A village in Vraja connected with Kṛṣṇa's family and pastimes.
body: Nanda-grāma is remembered here as a village in Vraja connected with Kṛṣṇa's family and pastimes. The village (grāma) of Nanda Mahārāja, renamed from Nandīśvara when Nanda moved back there from Chaṭīkarā after Kṛṣṇa was seven, since it was his capital. Vraja tradition describes the view from Nandīśvara Hill, where Kṛṣṇa's pranks can be recalled, and the route Uddhava travelled from Mathurā to Nandagrāma with Kṛṣṇa's messages for the Vraja-vāsīs. Nandagrāma is a key reference point for parikrama and for New Vraja-dhāma. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja, Uddhava. The name marks this as a hill sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Varṣāṇa
summary: A village in Vraja connected with Kṛṣṇa's family and pastimes.
body: Varsāṇā is the hill town associated with Rādhārāṇī's childhood home. It stands above the villages and groves of Vraja. The town is remembered for Rādhā's family and Her companions. Her parents and the nearby village of Nanda-grāma are part of the same story. The slopes and lanes are filled with places linked to Her pastimes. Kṛṣṇa's visits to Varsāṇā are recalled in the Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa narratives. The town is especially honoured during seasonal celebrations. Temples and stepping stones keep the memories present for visitors. Its elevated position makes it a landmark within the surrounding sacred landscape. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Yamunā
summary: The sacred river that flows through the land of Vraja.
body: The Yamunā is the river that forms the eastern boundary of much of Vraja. Its bank carries the memory of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and later pastimes. Vasudeva is remembered carrying the infant Kṛṣṇa across its waters to Nanda's home. The river is also tied to the story of Dhruva's austerity in Madhuvana. Kaliya's subduing took place in its waters near Vṛndāvana. Ghats along the river are used for bathing, worship and quiet remembrance. Forests such as Madhuvana and Kumudavana remember an older, winding course of the water. The river joins many separate sites into one sacred geography. Its presence shapes both the practical routes and the stories of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

Bathing there is more sacred than bathing in the Ganges, and bathing at Viśrāma-tīrtha, also called Ādi-varāha-tīrtha, is a hundred times more sacred still. Vajranābha established a temple here with Deities of Yamunā and Yamarāja, and it is visited by throngs of brothers and sisters on Bhrātṛ-dvitīyā. title: Sri Madana-mohana Temple
summary: Vṛndāvana temple of Śrī Rādhā-Madan Mohan, associated with Sanātana Gosvāmī and the Gauḍīya line from Śrī Caitanya.
body: Sri Madana-mohana Temple is remembered here as vṛndāvana temple of Śrī Rādhā-Madan Mohan, associated with Sanātana Gosvāmī and the Gauḍīya line from Śrī Caitanya. Sanātana Gosvāmī is named as the main Gosvāmī connected with this temple. Dīkṣā-guru: Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu; direct initiation is traditionally accepted in Gauḍīya traditions. Śikṣā-guru: also Śrī Caitanya. Lineage: Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Sanātana Gosvāmī. Sanātana was personally instructed for two months in Vārāṇasī by Mahāprabhu. Vajranābha tradition: Śrī Madana-Mohana was originally installed in Vṛndāvana and was later taken to Karauli. The area is identified with Vṛndāvana in this sacred circuit. The deity honoured at the site is Śrī Rādhā-Madan Mohan. Sanātana Gosvāmī is named as the main Gosvāmī connected with this temple. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Mana-sarovara
summary: Tradition distinguishes Manaḥ-sarovara, a lake in the Himalayas born from Brahmā's mind (manaḥ), from the Vraja lake Māna-sarovara, which people often confuse with it.
body: Mana-sarovara is remembered here as tradition distinguishes Manaḥ-sarovara, a lake in the Himalayas born from Brahmā's mind (manaḥ), from the Vraja lake Māna-sarovara, which people often confuse with it. A lake in Vraja created from Rādhā's tears of proud anger (māna) during a rāsa dance on a sandy shoal of the Yamunā, and bathing there is said to give a love like Hers. Kṛṣṇa called it a lake born of Her tears and just like His heart, while Rādhā said it was her heart, so it is also called Hṛdaya-sarovara. The Yamunā flows between this lake and Vṛndāvana, and tradition notes it should not be confused with Manaḥ-sarovara in the Himalayas. Māna-sarovara was created by Rādhā's tears of proud anger (māna) when she felt slighted during a rāsa dance on a sandy shoal of the Yamunā. Here the mention is mainly for clarification, not a pastime of its own. The area is identified with Vrindavana area in this sacred circuit. Bathing without offence in these two lakes fills a person with ecstatic love, and the trees, creepers, animals, and birds of the forest have also become filled with prema. In one pastime, Kṛṣṇa took the form of a varāha, or boar, to playfully frighten His friends, who fell down and offered prayers until the Lord revealed Himself and serenity returned.
