title: Datihā
summary: Ancient village founded by Vajranābha, marking where Kṛṣṇa defeated Dantavakra before returning to Vraja.
body: Datihā is remembered here as ancient village founded by Vajranābha, marking where Kṛṣṇa defeated Dantavakra before returning to Vraja. On the road from Satohā toward Nandagrāma, Datihā is counted among Vraja's oldest settlements, traditionally founded by Vajranābha. That founding connects the village with the early settlement of this part of Mathurā's domain. Tradition remembers it also as Dati-upavana, where Kṛṣṇa struck down Dantavakra and his brother Vidūratha, ending a mission to remove miscreants from the earth. Before crossing the Yamunā to meet His anxious kinsmen, the Lord set His weapons aside here. The adjoining Mayūra grove recalls a secret meeting of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, served by the gopīs: peacocks gathered, circled in contrary ranks, and joined the couple's dance, later refreshing themselves at Mayūra-kuṇḍa. Thus the village holds both the gravity of Kṛṣṇa's promised return to Vraja and the lighter wonder of forest creatures drawn into His līlā. The peacocks' calls were understood as proclaiming Kṛṣṇa's sway over all things and Rādhā's sway over Him. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Gandheśvara
summary: Fragrant garden near Koṭikā where Kṛṣṇa sampled perfumes and sought the scent most pleasing to Rādhā.
body: Gandheśvara is remembered here as fragrant garden near Koṭikā where Kṛṣṇa sampled perfumes and sought the scent most pleasing to Rādhā. Gandheśvara, also called Gaṇeśrā, lies beyond Koṭikā and is centred on Gandharva-kuṇḍa. Vraja's perfumers once tended flower gardens beside this water, distilling rose, jasmine, sandal, aguru, musk, khus, saffron and amber into oils for the Lord's bath and for offerings in temple and home. The garden's blossoms also furnished gifts of attar for Rādhā and Her friends. While the cows grazed nearby, Kṛṣṇa and the gopas tested these scents. Tradition recalls Him consulting Subala about an aroma that might soften Rādhā's contrary mood, and later appearing in female disguise to anoint Her wrists with attar. The boys' imitation of His example amused their parents. Devotees honour the lingering fragrance as a sign that even a humble craft can become service when offered to the divine couple. Even the scents noticed on Caitanya's later wanderings were compared with such gifts. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Chaṭīkarā
summary: Earlier dwelling of Nanda's family, remembered as the starting point of Kṛṣṇa's calf-herding boyhood pastimes.
body: Chaṭīkarā is remembered here as earlier dwelling of Nanda's family, remembered as the starting point of Kṛṣṇa's calf-herding boyhood pastimes. Chaṭīkarā is revered as a partial manifestation of Nandagrāma, Kṛṣṇa's original home. Parjanya Mahārāja settled his family near Nandīśvara, but left that region because of Keśī's harassment; Nanda later moved back from Chaṭīkarā when Kṛṣṇa was seven, and the place became Nandagrāma. The site is also linked to the boyhood pastime of Bakāsura. One day Kṛṣṇa and the gopas drove their calves from Chaṭīkarā to the broad lake at Baka-sthala in Khadiravana. The demon swallowed the Lord, was forced to release Him, and was torn apart as His friends watched. Their alarm at the giant bird and Kṛṣṇa's burning heat within its throat belong to the remembered scene. Devotees therefore remember Chaṭīkarā both as a household stage of Nanda's life and as the threshold of Kṛṣṇa's fearless exploits among the cows. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Dakṣiṇa (Jakhīna)
summary: Village between Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā and Toṣa where Rādhā's rare submission and Balarāma's victory are remembered.
body: Dakṣiṇa (Jakhīna) is remembered here as village between Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā and Toṣa where Rādhā's rare submission and Balarāma's victory are remembered. Dakṣiṇa lies halfway between Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā and Toṣa, and is dear to Kṛṣṇa because here Rādhā, usually contrary and resistant, became wholly gentle and yielding to Him for confidential reasons. Such a mood is rare, and tradition treats the place as especially cherished by the Lord. Its second name, Jakhīna, recalls a yakṣiṇī who disturbed the locality until Balarāma subdued her. Several lakes mark the village: Balarāma-kuṇḍa and Revatī-kuṇḍa honour the elder brother and His consort, while Reṇukā-kuṇḍa and Jamadagni-kuṇḍa remember the sage who once dwelt there. Pilgrims on this leg of the circuit thus find both an intimate lesson in Rādhā's love and a witness to Balarāma's protective strength. Jamadagni's association also prompts reflection on sages who discover the Absolute Truth as a cowherd boy in Vraja. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Nima-grāma
summary: Grove facing Sauṅkarāi where elderly gopīs honoured Kṛṣṇa after He lifted Govardhana Hill.
body: Nima-grāma is remembered here as grove facing Sauṅkarāi where elderly gopīs honoured Kṛṣṇa after He lifted Govardhana Hill. Nima-grāma rests in a small nima forest facing Sauṅkarāi. The place is linked to the aftermath of Kṛṣṇa's lifting of Govardhana: His mother, grandmothers and other senior gopīs embraced Him, wiped away His perspiration, and offered lamps amid tears, caring more for Him than for their own families endangered by Indra's flood. Their loving worship is remembered in the older name Nirmañcana-grāma, which gradually became Nima-grāma. Though the grove once nestled against Girirāja, the hill's apparent shrinkage has left it at some distance today. Later, Nimbārka Svāmī lived here, worshipping Kṛṣṇa in the Kumāra-sampradāya; tradition links his name to a nima tree and a wondrous prolonging of daylight. Behind the village, devotees meditate on the Yoga-pīṭha before proceeding toward Rāmeśvara Mahādeva at the rear approach to Rādhā-kuṇḍa. Figures linked with this place include Indra. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Gāṅṭhuli
summary: Village where Gopāla left Govardhana for three days so Caitanya Mahāprabhu could behold Him.
body: Gāṅṭhuli is remembered here as village where Gopāla left Govardhana for three days so Caitanya Mahāprabhu could behold Him. Gāṅṭhuli is honoured for a deliberate pastime of mercy. Because Mahāprabhu would not step onto Govardhana, Gopāla arranged a rumour of approaching soldiers and was moved to a brāhmaṇa's house in this village, where His worship continued in secret. Hearing the news at Govinda-kuṇḍa, Caitanya detoured from his hill circumambulation and saw the Deity. He stayed three days, chanting and dancing in ecstasy, then accompanied Gopāla back to the foot of the hill on the fourth day. There He bowed without treading on Girirāja. Tradition compares this kindness to Gopāla's month-long audience with Rūpa Gosvāmī and other Gosvāmīs in Mathurā. The village also recalls Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's Holī sport at Gulāla-kuṇḍa, where coloured powders still seem to surface in the water. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Beheja
summary: Named stop on both the Govardhana-side and outer circuits of Vraja's sacred geography.
body: Beheja is remembered here as named stop on both the Govardhana-side and outer circuits of Vraja's sacred geography. Beheja is honoured after Gāṅṭhuli and before Ḍīg on the Govardhana stretch, and again on the eighty-four-krośa circuit between Samāi and Ḍīg. Tradition offers no distinct līlā for this village; its importance lies in being counted among the līlā-sthānas that pilgrims remember while walking. Different Vaiṣṇava lists vary in sequence without thereby losing validity. Such listings are not mere geography. Each named halt directs attention to Kṛṣṇa's presence in the fields, roads and villages of Vraja, where the cowherd life unfolded in ordinary view. Devotees therefore respect Beheja as part of the sacred chain of places, even where no separate story is told, and include it in meditation on the complete circuit of the dhāma. Both Bhauma Vṛndāvana and New Vraja-dhāma have their own such lists. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Sehu
summary: Traditionally named halt between Kedāranātha and Indrolī on the Govardhana-side parikrama route.
body: Sehu is remembered here as traditionally named halt between Kedāranātha and Indrolī on the Govardhana-side parikrama route. Sehu is honoured between Kedāranātha and Indrolī, on the segment associated with the Govardhana circuit. No individual narrative is given for it. Its sanctity comes from inclusion in the circumambulation of the dhāma, where villages, groves and waters are honoured as settings of Kṛṣṇa's cowherd life. Walking such a route, devotees move through a landscape mapped by memory rather than by story alone. Sehu thus remains a quiet named station in Vraja's sacred route, inviting respectful recollection of the Lord's presence among the other places named nearby. The appendix presenting such lists notes that sequences may differ by tradition or practical need, yet each name remains a worthy object of remembrance. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. The name marks this as a village sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Satavāsa
summary: Eastern petal where Rādhā worships the sun and Satrājit once sought wealth at Sūrya-kuṇḍa.
body: Satavāsa is remembered here as eastern petal where Rādhā worships the sun and Satrājit once sought wealth at Sūrya-kuṇḍa. Satavāsa, east of Kāmaravana, is the first place in the dhāma to receive the rising sun, fittingly because Śrīmatī Rādhā is remembered as worshipping the sun here. Beside Sūrya-kuṇḍa, Satrājit built a temple and sought riches and a child through austere worship. Tradition links that worship to the later Syamantaka episode: the jewel and Satyabhāmā, an aṁśa of Rādhā, came to him from the sun god, but greed and display ruined him. The sun god is said to have arranged for Satrājit to deliver Satyabhāmā to Kṛṣṇa in Dvārakā; that gift, meant as blessing, became a snare through attachment. Devotees honour the lake and its sunrise setting as a place where simple devotion to the divine couple is preferred over ceremonial ambition. The name marks this as a temple site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Vanacārī (Vanacāriyā)
summary: Garden near Sītā-Rāma where gopas debated whether Kṛṣṇa was a cowherd or forest dweller.
body: Vanacārī (Vanacāriyā) is remembered here as garden near Sītā-Rāma where gopas debated whether Kṛṣṇa was a cowherd or forest dweller. South of Sītā-Rāma lies the garden called Vanacāriyā. The gopas had brought their cows to rich pastures, while Kṛṣṇa slipped away, saying He wished to see the forest—a plea some boys understood as a meeting with the gopīs. In His absence, one level-headed boy argued that Kṛṣṇa belonged to the forest: He returned from the Yamunā's groves garlanded and finely dressed, used Nandagrāma almost as a dressing room, and slipped out at night. The others insisted He was a gopa like themselves. The word vana-cārī echoed through the trees until Kṛṣṇa's flute silenced the debate and His arrival dissolved all doubt. The place preserves the playful closeness of friends who could question His identity yet could not live without Him. Their arguing ends in embraces, not in any settled verdict. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Gendokhara (Gendo)
summary: Level field near Nandagrāma where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma played ball with the gopas.
body: Gendokhara (Gendo) is remembered here as level field near Nandagrāma where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma played ball with the gopas. Following the path around Nandagrāma, one reaches a level playing field called Gendokhara, a place where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma played ball. The boys came here after the morning milking or stopped on the way to pasture; the game belongs to the easy rhythm of village life. Once Rādhā watched from a nearby bush as Kṛṣṇa sported with His friends. From hiding She wished She too might play with Him with the same freedom the gopas enjoyed. Tradition explains that the boys' viśrambha lets them treat Kṛṣṇa as an equal, while the gopīs' deeper love must remain less public. The field therefore recalls both innocent play and the longing hidden behind Vraja's open camaraderie. Beyond it lies Madhusūdanavana, where bees drone beside Madhusūdana-kuṇḍa beneath a bakula tree. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Chaṭa
summary: Named halt in the Nanda-grāma list after Khadiravana, before Yāvaṭā and Kokilavana.
body: Chaṭa is remembered here as named halt in the Nanda-grāma list after Khadiravana, before Yāvaṭā and Kokilavana. Chaṭa is honoured after Khadiravana and before Yāvaṭā and Kokilavana, in the section associated with Nanda's village and its surrounding woods. No separate pastime is told about the place itself. Its holiness rests on being part of that remembered route, where each halting point keeps alive some feature of Kṛṣṇa's life with the cows—here the move from the lake and acacia woods toward the groves where the boys grazed calves and played. The nearby lake at Khadiravana is where the Bakāsura pastime unfolded. Devotees honour Chaṭa as one link in the chain of sacred locations, allowing the whole landscape to speak of the Lord's childhood pastimes even without a distinct narrative. In this way it belongs to the geography of memory that shapes parikrama. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kāmara
summary: Secluded winter meeting place near Kāmaravana linked with Kṛṣṇa's care for thirsty cowherd boys.
body: Kāmara is remembered here as secluded winter meeting place near Kāmaravana linked with Kṛṣṇa's care for thirsty cowherd boys. Kāmara, also called Kāmera, lies a short distance from Kāmaravana near Durvāsā-kuṇḍa. One winter day Kṛṣṇa chose its seclusion for a meeting with Rādhā; He spread His blanket on a rock and waited, restless at Her delay. Kāmaravana's name itself is linked both to Kṛṣṇa's eager mood there and to a blanket He left behind. The area also remembers His care for the gopas. Near Phakarapura, absorbed in play, the boys suddenly cried out that they were thirsty. Kṛṣṇa played a melody and water rose from the ground to form a small lake, so they drank from cupped hands and forgot their distress in delight. Kāmara thus joins two moods of Vraja līlā: the Lord's eager waiting for Rādhā and His prompt response to the smallest need of His friends. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Rāsolī
summary: Secluded grove by Rāsa-kuṇḍa where Kṛṣṇa danced with the gopīs beneath a spreading banyan.
body: Rāsolī is remembered here as secluded grove by Rāsa-kuṇḍa where Kṛṣṇa danced with the gopīs beneath a spreading banyan. Rāsolī, also called Raṅkolī, takes its name from the rāsa dance Kṛṣṇa performed on the bank of Rāsa-kuṇḍa. Near Kośīkalā yet away from roads and markets, it remained a quiet retreat where the Lord summoned the gopīs with His flute when they visited their parents around Varṣāṇā. A huge banyan shaped the dance. Its canopy hid the circle, while its hanging roots made the partners weave in zigzag paths rather than simple rings. Afterwards they bathed in the kuṇḍa, played in the water, and rested in arbours made from the tree's roots. So intense was the joy that boughs and roots seemed to sway along with the dancers. Some traditions also associate the village with Rādhā's dear friends Tuṅgavidyā or Indulekhā, both honoured by devotees. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Dahgaon
summary: Village named between Rāsolī and Koṭaravana on the woodland part of the Vraja circuit.
body: Dahgaon is remembered here as village named between Rāsolī and Koṭaravana on the woodland part of the Vraja circuit. Dahgaon is named in the traditional list of pastime places after Rāsolī and before Koṭaravana, within the woodland stretch of the Varṣāṇā-side route. Tradition does not narrate a distinct pastime for this village. Its place in the sequence is nevertheless significant: it helps mark the passage from the rāsa grove into the dense forests associated with Rādhā's western landscape. Pilgrims who keep such a route in mind move through Vraja as through a sacred map, each name prompting remembrance of the Lord's presence. Dahgaon is therefore honoured as part of that forested setting, without any invented tale attached to it. Its position between a rāsa grove and a hollow-tree forest fixes its place in that remembered landscape, serving as a quiet landmark for meditation. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Koṭaravana
summary: Ancient hollow-tree forest near Kośīvana where gopas hid, played Holī and sought milk.
body: Koṭaravana is remembered here as ancient hollow-tree forest near Kośīvana where gopas hid, played Holī and sought milk. Koṭaravana is an ancient forest between Kośīvana and Śeṣaśāyī, named for the hollow trunks (koṭara) of its aged trees. Kṛṣṇa brought His cows here to graze, and the boys hid in those hollows or splashed one another with Holī colours. Once a long morning of play left the gopas famished and the lunch late. On Balarāma's advice they went to the neighbouring village now called Paya-grāma and were given milk. Nearby Dadhi-grāma recalls Kṛṣṇa's seizure of the gopīs' yogurt offering at Dadhi-kuṇḍa, which He shared with His friends before the deity's smiling image. The forest also has a Sūrya-kuṇḍa where Rādhā and Her companions worshipped the sun, linking its shade and waters to several strands of Vraja līlā. Kharero, on the western side, recalls Balarāma's return journey from Dvārakā. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kośīkalā (Kośī)
summary: Holy town and Nanda's granary identified with Kuśasthalī, whose Gomatī-kuṇḍa grants Dvārakā's vision.
body: Kośīkalā (Kośī) is remembered here as holy town and Nanda's granary identified with Kuśasthalī, whose Gomatī-kuṇḍa grants Dvārakā's vision. Kośīkalā, or Kośī, stands in Kośīvana as a major granary belonging to Nanda Mahārāja. Vaiṣṇava scholars identify it with Kuśasthalī and Dvārakā Purī present in Vraja. When Nanda wished to visit the distant holy city on the Gomatī, Kṛṣṇa persuaded him that the same sanctity was at hand. At Gomatī-kuṇḍa the Vraja-vāsīs bathed and, by the lake's grace, saw the ocean, Gomatī-ghāṭa and Dvārakā itself; from then on a visit here was held equal to that pilgrimage. Tradition also remembers the gopīs' outing to bathe in this lake: Kṛṣṇa joined the party and drew them through forest paths into a long, affectionate detour, turning an errand into a pastime. Kośīvana's own name arises from Rādhā's teasing question to Kṛṣṇa at a locked grove: ko 'si. The approach is praised for its unusual quiet and wide views. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Ūjānī
summary: Yamunā-side place where Kṛṣṇa's flute-song turned the river back toward His feet.
body: Ūjānī is remembered here as yamunā-side place where Kṛṣṇa's flute-song turned the river back toward His feet. Ūjānī stands at the start of the riverbank section that continues toward Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa through Khelanavana. Its name is linked to the Yamunā's reversal: tradition points to unusual cross-currents and whirlpools as witnesses of a time when Kṛṣṇa's melody made the river change course and flow toward Him, offering lotuses on its waves. The episode belongs to Kṛṣṇa's experiments with melodies after Dhenukāsura's defeat, when He sought a tune to draw the gopīs, who remained outwardly indifferent after their transfer to their husbands' homes. Here the waters responded before the girls did. Devotees pray that the same flute-song which redirected the Yamunā may turn their wandering hearts toward Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet. Khelanavana, the riverside stretch from Ūjānī to Gopī-ghāṭa, is named for Kṛṣṇa's and Balarāma's frequent games with Their friends. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Vāndī
summary: Village of Nanda's ancestral worship where Durgā's two forms served the baby Kṛṣṇa.
body: Vāndī is remembered here as village of Nanda's ancestral worship where Durgā's two forms served the baby Kṛṣṇa. Vāndī appears on both the forest circuit, between Lohavana and Baladeva, and the outer circumambulation near Kayalo and Dhana-grāma. Tradition remembers it as the place where Nanda's ancestors honoured Durgā in her two forms, named Vāndī and Ānandī. Tradition connects the site with Kṛṣṇa's hair-cutting ceremony. Eager to keep seeing the child, the two goddesses took human form and performed humble service, making and delivering cow-dung patties from the pastures near Gokula; in that guise they were blessed to see and play with Him in Nanda's courtyard. In Bhauma Vṛndāvana Vāndī is a dark four-armed image, while red, eight-armed Ānandī battles the Mahiṣa demon; a lake stands behind each shrine. The tradition was preserved locally even when other sites grew obscure. Figures linked with this place include Balarāma, Nanda Mahārāja. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Barifā
summary: Boundary village on the dhāma's edge remembered for the gopas' hearty winter eating.
body: Barifā is remembered here as boundary village on the dhāma's edge remembered for the gopas' hearty winter eating. Barifā sits at the end of one of the dhāma's petals, near the boundary route used for circumambulation. Tradition groups it with Vatsavana, Soṅkh and Mālapura as places connected with Kṛṣṇa's eating pastimes, especially in the winter month of Pauṣa, when the cowherd boys' appetite was keenest and the day's merrymaking especially lively. At Barifā the gopas are remembered as overeating, replenishing the energy spent in herding, games and escapes from demons. Their fare came from forest fruit, lunch packs from home and dairy stores raided from the village—yogurt, mākhana, rabrī and sweet rice. The place therefore keeps the homely, joyful side of Vraja līlā: Kṛṣṇa's presence turns even a simple meal into a feast that nourishes body and soul. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kotharā
summary: Turning point near Vatsavana where a kuṇḍa refreshed Kṛṣṇa's cows before their homeward walk.
body: Kotharā is remembered here as turning point near Vatsavana where a kuṇḍa refreshed Kṛṣṇa's cows before their homeward walk. A little beyond Soṅkh, Kotharā is where the New Vraja-dhāma circumambulation route bends sharply toward Kāmyavana along a line of trees dividing two valleys. The spot marks the transition between the eastern petals of the dhāma and the more frequented western ones. Kotharā-kuṇḍa supplied fresh water and rest for Kṛṣṇa's cows before they returned from this far corner. The pastures beyond the village were among their favourites, and a temple of Lord Nārāyaṇa now stands there. Nearby Soṅkh-kuṇḍa is said to retain the aroma of the gopīs' cooking. Nearby Mālīpura recalls florists who reserved their finest garlands for Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma and were taught that worship is complete when His dear friends are honoured too. Thus a practical need of the herd is folded into the sacred route. The name marks this as a temple site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Devaśīrṣa
summary: Place where devas offered lofty hymns to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, their flowers forming a kuṇḍa.
body: Devaśīrṣa is remembered here as place where devas offered lofty hymns to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, their flowers forming a kuṇḍa. At Devaśīrṣa the demigods are remembered as offering solemn hymns to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma while the brothers grazed cattle in the nearby pastures. Flowers showered by the devas and their wives are said to have gathered into Devaśīrṣa-kuṇḍa. The brothers' carefree behaviour puzzled celestial onlookers unaccustomed to cowherd play. Tradition contrasts the devas, who remained conscious of their cosmic offices and could not approach the Lord, with sages at neighbouring Muniśīrṣa-sthāna. Those munis relinquished false designations; their heads, bowed in Vṛndāvana's dust, awakened the devotion that brought them into Kṛṣṇa's presence. The place thus highlights a quiet paradox of Vraja: exalted praise alone is less effective than humble surrender to the Lord playing as a cowherd boy. Nearby Mālīpura's florists had likewise been taught that serving the Lord's dear ones completes worship. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Pramodana (Pramodavana)
summary: Woodland village where Kṛṣṇa's presence turned the gopīs' tears of separation into joy.
body: Pramodana (Pramodavana) is remembered here as woodland village where Kṛṣṇa's presence turned the gopīs' tears of separation into joy. Pramodavana and its village Pramodana lie beyond Ghāṭā on the approach to Kāmyavana. Both names point to the delight Kṛṣṇa gave the gopīs on two occasions when they came searching for Him. Once they wandered here without finding their beloved, until their tears gathered into a rivulet whose dark, warm water caught His attention as He walked along with Balarāma, the boys and the cows. He slipped away from His companions and appeared among the weeping girls, expanding Himself so that each one received His personal care. He dried their faces with the edge of His cloth and gave them the company they longed for. Later, at Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa, clouds mirrored in the water stirred such feelings that the gopīs fainted; Kṛṣṇa revived them with His touch and voice. A deity of Sudāmā is honoured there, and Caraṇa-kuṇḍa in the same forest is revered as sanctified by the Lord's feet. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Āṭora
summary: Secluded grove where Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and the cows lost a full day to play.
body: Āṭora is remembered here as secluded grove where Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and the cows lost a full day to play. Āṭora lies off the travelled route, tucked between the roads toward Kāmyavana and Varṣāṇā. Here Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma joined the cowherd boys in games so absorbing that boys and cattle alike forgot the hour. A full twenty-four hours elapsed before Nanda Mahārāja found them: the parents had searched through the night in two armed parties, and Yaśodā had feared some demon had taken her son. When Nanda reached the grove, the brothers were still playing and the cows were watching them as though caught in the same spell. The boys thought only moments had passed and were amazed to hear how long they had been away. Tradition adds that a still greater span, a night of Brahmā, had slipped by, so the place measures Kṛṣṇa's līlā against another scale of time altogether. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Hara-Nārāyaṇa
summary: Paths where Kṛṣṇa startled His friends by appearing as four-armed Nārāyaṇa mid-play.
body: Hara-Nārāyaṇa is remembered here as paths where Kṛṣṇa startled His friends by appearing as four-armed Nārāyaṇa mid-play. Between Dāna and Ṭeṛh-kadamba, Kṛṣṇa once slipped from sight while the gopas played. A fallen peacock feather put the searchers on His trail, and near a solitary tree He revealed Himself as four-armed Nārāyaṇa, with crown, gem and the emblems of mastery in His hands. The boys stopped short in awe and bowed with joined palms while He smiled at them like a fond father. Unable to keep up the comedy, Kṛṣṇa resumed His cowherd form, called out that He had fooled them and ran toward the grazing cows; the boys sprang after Him. Vraja tradition dwells on small human touches, a flute tucked under His belt and a turban left in a branch, around that grand appearance. The gopīs also examined the report of His extra arms here, their testing arising from affection rather than defiance. The name marks this as a sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Umrao
summary: Willow-shaded spot where Rādhā was crowned and Kṛṣṇa gave Lokanātha the Rādhā-vinoda Deity.
body: Umrao is remembered here as willow-shaded spot where Rādhā was crowned and Kṛṣṇa gave Lokanātha the Rādhā-vinoda Deity. Just south of Rahela, Umrao rests beneath a weeping willow. Devotees honour it as the place where Paurṇamāsī and the goddesses crowned Śrī Rādhā queen of Vṛndāvana, while Kiśorī-kuṇḍa keeps the memory of Her ceremonial bath. The name also carries the sense of Unmatta-rādhā-sthalī, where Rādhā was overcome with happiness at Her sovereignty. Lokanātha Gosvāmī stayed near that lake, secretly yearning for a Deity of Kṛṣṇa. The Lord appeared holding His own image, placed it in the trembling hands of His servant as Rādhā-vinoda and vanished. When the gosvāmī worried about shelter and worship, the Deity said He would dwell with him in the forest and only asked to be fed; rice on a banana leaf became the first offering. Lokanātha kept the small form in a cloth bag at his neck rather than accept a cottage. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Yamunā-mātā
summary: Riverbank halt where the Yamunā is honoured as mother and linked to Kṛṣṇa's moonlit rāsa.
body: Yamunā-mātā is remembered here as riverbank halt where the Yamunā is honoured as mother and linked to Kṛṣṇa's moonlit rāsa. Yamunā-mātā is a named station on the riverbank stretch of the circuit, between Mukharāi and the turn into the Govardhana lists. Devotees bow to the Yamunā here as a mother whose waters carry Kṛṣṇa's pastimes. The passage does not recount an event at this ghāṭa itself; instead it follows the same branch of the river downstream and then inland. That branch reaches Parāsaulī, where Kṛṣṇa arranged a spring rāsa for His eternally liberated companions after the autumn festival had left them unsatisfied. The moon rose unusually high so Govardhana's peaks would not block the view, and Kṛṣṇa played beneath a spreading banyan, a second Vaṁśīvaṭa, in melody only those gopīs could hear. The river then bends toward Nandagrāma and Soṅkh, joining this halt to a longer chain of līlā places. The name marks this as a village sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Pāpaḍī (Pāpaḍīvana)
summary: Petal grove where the gopīs adorned Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa with blossom-crafted ornaments.
body: Pāpaḍī (Pāpaḍīvana) is remembered here as petal grove where the gopīs adorned Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa with blossom-crafted ornaments. South of Kanabāḍī, Pāpaḍī is the central grove of flowering Pāpaḍīvana. The gopīs gathered here to welcome Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, shaping soft petals into garlands, crowns, a throne, an umbrella and festoons. Such delicate work demanded patience, and Vraja tradition reads that care as a sign of affection rather than simple decoration. When the divine couple saw the arrangements, They were deeply touched and agreed to whatever Their friends requested, including garlands of petal work. Tradition praises these offerings as the finest essence of flower worship, since blossoms are Vraja's natural wealth and Kṛṣṇa, as Vanamālī, takes joy in them. The grove is remembered as a place where humble forest materials became a full declaration of the gopīs' love. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Didāvalī
summary: Village repeated on two Vraja circuits, honoured as a named stop near Khoṅha and Kotharā.
body: Didāvalī is remembered here as village repeated on two Vraja circuits, honoured as a named stop near Khoṅha and Kotharā. Didāvalī appears twice in the traditional routes preserved here: on the outer Bhauma Vṛndāvana round between Ḍīg and Khoṅha, and on the route running from Kotharā through Ḍīg toward Ādi-badri and Paśupā. No līlā is attached to the village itself, so its sanctity comes from inclusion in the circular path that honours the entire dhāma. Those who keep that round pass through orchards, groves and cowherd settlements, every name recalling some part of Kṛṣṇa's life in Vraja. Khoṅha nearby is remembered as the gopīs' playing field, and farther on stand Ādi-badri and Paśupā, where the cows found the hidden brothers. Set among such stations, Didāvalī marks the continuity of the walk rather than a single episode. Its repeated listing shows how the tradition regards the land itself as holy, not only the spots where a particular story is told. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Paśupā
summary: Grove where clever cows tracked Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Their hiding place.
body: Paśupā is remembered here as grove where clever cows tracked Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Their hiding place. Paśupā is a grove inside Paśupāvana, south of Bhayarī. Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma once concealed Themselves while the boys played ball and tag. When every cow had been counted and the brothers were still missing, the gopas grew frantic, calling Their names and asking the trees and deer; the cattle rose, called out to the brothers and started searching as though for lost calves. Several cows followed the brothers' bodily fragrance, and the boys followed the cows' hoofprints into the thicket, where they found the two delighted by their trick. The name joins paśu, cattle, with pā, the track, and Vraja tradition draws a lesson from it: one reaches Kṛṣṇa by walking behind those who already know Him. Afterwards Devaprastha begged His friend never to hide again, for life without that sight felt like death. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Phalain
summary: Area near Kośīkalā where Holī re-enacts Prahlāda's deliverance from a burning pyre.
body: Phalain is remembered here as area near Kośīkalā where Holī re-enacts Prahlāda's deliverance from a burning pyre. Phalain lies to one side of the Kośīkalā route, outside the official parikrama line yet well known for Prahlāda-kuṇḍa. Each year the Holikā-dahan is observed on its bank: an effigy of Hiraṇyakaśipu's sister is burned after dark, and colours are thrown the following morning to celebrate Prahlāda's victory. The story recalled is of a boy whose only shelter was chanting Kṛṣṇa's names. Holikā sat with him on the pyre, guarded by a boon against fire, yet the flames consumed her while he stepped out untouched; his strength was surrender, not any occult power. Tradition says Kṛṣṇa remembered this faith each spring in Vraja and later invoked it when assuring Arjuna that His devotee never perishes. Visitors therefore meditate here on protection that springs from reliance on the Lord. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. Figures linked with this place include Arjuna. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kerala
summary: Grazing field where Kṛṣṇa rested on a tree root and dreamed of Rādhā.
body: Kerala is remembered here as grazing field where Kṛṣṇa rested on a tree root and dreamed of Rādhā. Kerala is an open field on the grazing round that begins at Loṭana-kuṇḍa. At its southern edge a spot called Caukī is marked by a tree with an exposed root. Weary from walking, Kṛṣṇa used that root as a seat, leaned back against the trunk and closed His eyes, dreaming of the meeting with Rādhā set for later that night. The place holds two moods together: the ordinary work of herding and the hidden life of love. Nearby Rāndhera recalls another moment on the same round, when Kṛṣṇa asked gopīs carrying water for a drink and praised the sweetness of a lake named for Rādhā. Tradition also notes that the holy spots north of Kerala and those reached farther out form a continuous field of pilgrimage in New Vraja-dhāma. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Gopī-ghāṭa
summary: Yamunā bathing ghāṭa where the unmarried gopīs performed their Kātyāyanī-vrata ablutions before Kṛṣṇa's arrival.
body: Gopī-ghāṭa is remembered here as yamunā bathing ghāṭa where the unmarried gopīs performed their Kātyāyanī-vrata ablutions before Kṛṣṇa's arrival. Downstream from Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa, Gopī-ghāṭa is one of three sites in the Kātyāyanī pastime: Tapovana, where the young women undertook austerities, this ghāṭa, used for their river ablutions, and Cīra-ghāṭa, the later site of the garment pastime. The girls in that story are unmarried friends of Dhanyā, not Rādhā's own circle. Vṛndā-devī, appearing as an ascetic, taught them the vow; for a month they rose before dawn, bathed in the cold river, worshipped Kātyāyanī and went home, secretly asking for Kṛṣṇa as husband. At this ghāṭa they laid aside their shawls, entered the water in cotton bathing dress and performed the prescribed rites despite steam rising from the winter river. The spot preserves the memory of that quiet resolve before the riverbank play began. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. The nearby Yamunā ties this spot to other sacred places along the river. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Kayalo
summary: First named halt after Viśrāma-ghāṭa on the outer Bhauma Vṛndāvana parikrama circuit.
body: Kayalo is remembered here as first named halt after Viśrāma-ghāṭa on the outer Bhauma Vṛndāvana parikrama circuit. Kayalo stands immediately after Viśrāma-ghāṭa in the list of Bhauma Vṛndāvana, the round that both begins and ends at that resting ghāṭa before passing Vāndī, Dhana-grāma and the great forests of Vraja. Tradition offers no līlā for Kayalo itself; what the tradition preserves is its position in the walk. Devotees circling this route honour the entire arc of Kṛṣṇa's life here: departure from the cowherd villages, the woods of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, the Yamunā's shore and the return to Viśrāma-ghāṭa. The following stations include Vāndī and Dhana-grāma, the village at the edge of Nanda's domain where Balarāma is still revered. A name such as Kayalo thus serves as a marker on a sacred map, holding even a modest settlement within the sphere of worship. Standing so near the start, it is the first step into that remembered circle. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Dhana-grāma
summary: Village at the tip of Tālavana marking Nanda's border, where Balarāma is worshipped.
body: Dhana-grāma is remembered here as village at the tip of Tālavana marking Nanda's border, where Balarāma is worshipped. The far end of Tālavana marks the limit of Nanda Mahārāja's domain, and the village at that boundary is Dhana-grāma, where Balarāma continues to be honoured. The adjoining forest, named for its palms, recalls the defeat of Dhenuka; once the demons were gone, the gopas could freely eat and throw the tāla fruit. Kṛṣṇa also brought forth the Vetra-gaṅgā spring with His dancing stick when the gopīs grew thirsty after a dance. Caitanya Mahāprabhu likewise visited Tālavana, honoured Balarāma as Dhenuka-mardī and bathed in that pure water. Tradition places Dhana-grāma both on the outer Bhauma Vṛndāvana list, between Vāndī and Tālavana, and on another circuit after Madhuvana. Its holiness is that of a borderland: the edge of the cowherd kingdom kept in affectionate regard because the elder brother is revered there. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu, Nanda Mahārāja. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Soṅkh
summary: Boundary halt where the gopīs' cooking fragrance drew Kṛṣṇa and Madhu to lunch.
body: Soṅkh is remembered here as boundary halt where the gopīs' cooking fragrance drew Kṛṣṇa and Madhu to lunch. Soṅkh belongs to the boundary places of the sīmā-parikrama, a group associated with eating during Pauṣa, when the cowherds' digestion and appetites were keenest. At Barifā the boys overate, at Vatsavana they complained of hunger, and here the scent of Rādhā's spicing reached Kṛṣṇa and Madhumaṅgala while the gopīs cooked, pretending they did not wish to feed anyone. Shyness kept the women from speaking openly of their wish, and contrariness made them deny it even while cooking. Gentle persistence won the two boys an invitation, and the clearing where the meal was taken, with Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā retiring later to a kuñja, is remembered as Soṅkh. Temples and lakes mark the area, among them Soṅkh-kuṇḍa, said to retain the aroma of that cooking even now. The outer list places it between Kumudavana and Vatsa-grāma, and another route after Barifā. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. The name marks this as a temple site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Vatsa-grāma
summary: Village on the outer route linked with Vatsavana, its hungry gopas and sacred lakes.
body: Vatsa-grāma is remembered here as village on the outer route linked with Vatsavana, its hungry gopas and sacred lakes. Vatsa-grāma is named once in the traditional list, between Soṅkh and Samāi on the Bhauma Vṛndāvana round. No episode is told about the village, but its name directs attention to Vatsavana, woodland of the calf pastimes, where the boys came in hunger with no lunch in hand, and where Brahmā was later bewildered by Kṛṣṇa's expansions among the herd. Tradition also mentions lakes there, such as Rabrī-kuṇḍa and Śaṅkara-kuṇḍa, which houses a Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa shrine. Nearby Soṅkh belongs to the same group of boundary spots where fragrance and food draw the Lord, while Samāi is honoured for the disguise He assumed to approach Rādhā. Vatsa-grāma is kept as a link in that sequence, a point on the path where the daily rounds of calves, cows and cowherds are recalled. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Samāi
summary: Garden by Śyāma-ḍhāk where Kṛṣṇa disguised as a gopī to melt Rādhā's anger.
body: Samāi is remembered here as garden by Śyāma-ḍhāk where Kṛṣṇa disguised as a gopī to melt Rādhā's anger. Samāi is a garden on the edge of Śyāma-ḍhāk, its name drawn from Śyāmā-sakhī. After a rāsa festival at Apsarāvana, Rādhā was displeased with Kṛṣṇa's arrangements and withdrew to pout in that secluded grove. When His efforts to console Her met only cold silence, Viśākhā advised a more tactful approach, and Kṛṣṇa came dressed as that gopī. The disguise caught Rādhā's attention and turned Her indifference into longing. The garden thus belongs to the delicate līlās of reconciliation. Nearby Sutalavana carries another farewell memory: the chariot taking Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā turned out of sight near Samāi while Lauṭhā watched and promised to wait for His friend's return. Devotees who walk the outer path here hold both the intimate quarrel of lovers and the sorrow of parting. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Khoṅha
summary: Playing field where Rādhā and the gopīs played kho-kho before Caitanya's samādhi grove.
body: Khoṅha is remembered here as playing field where Rādhā and the gopīs played kho-kho before Caitanya's samādhi grove. Khoṅha is recalled as the open field where Rādhā and Her companions played kho-kho, a chasing game akin to tag and a softer echo of the old heroic game played from chariots. Tradition delights in the divine couple watching one another with curiosity as They abandon themselves to such childish sport, each relishing the other's freedom in play. In New Vraja-dhāma this field is indicated by the open space facing Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī's samādhi; Jīva Gosvāmī is said to have brought his ashes from Rādhā-kuṇḍa for a second shrine. The eastern side represents Samādhivana, where the samādhis of Caitanya Mahāprabhu's sixty-four principal associates are remembered, one shrine here standing for all. Pilgrims bowing or circling at Khoṅha therefore honour both the gopīs' game and the saints who sanctified the same ground. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Bādalī
summary: Orchard where a summoned cloud shaded Kṛṣṇa and the boys from the midday heat.
body: Bādalī is remembered here as orchard where a summoned cloud shaded Kṛṣṇa and the boys from the midday heat. Bādalī is a forest orchard reached after the events at Paśupā, where Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd boys were tending cattle on a summer day. At noon the heat became unbearable, so they rested in the deepest shade: Kṛṣṇa lay with His head in a friend's lap while others fanned Him with a blossoming branch and massaged His hands and feet. A boy at His side moaned that even breathing was difficult and asked whether the Lord could do something. Kṛṣṇa played a melody that drew a cloud overhead; it spread like an umbrella, shut out the glare and released fine, flower-like drops. Within moments the grove felt like spring, the boys forgot their distress and the cows rose to graze in the cool rain. The place remembers how He answers even small complaints from His friends. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Pāi-grāma
summary: Village named on two Vraja routes between Bhojana-thālī, Pinthānā, Sītā-Rāma and Nīgānyā.
body: Pāi-grāma is remembered here as village named on two Vraja routes between Bhojana-thālī, Pinthānā, Sītā-Rāma and Nīgānyā. Pāi-grāma appears in the Bhauma Vṛndāvana list after Bhojana-thālī and before Pinthānā, and in a second route between Sītā-Rāma and Nīgānyā. Tradition gives it no narrative of its own, so its meaning comes from the places that neighbour it on the path. At Bhojana-thālī, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma once fed the famished gopas after a victory over Vyomāsura; the stone still bears the marks of His plate and the white streak of Balarāma's spilled kṣīra, beside the lake called Kṣīra-sāgara. Farther on, Nīgānyā recalls the gopīs stopping Kṛṣṇa to question His supposed shortcut on their way to Kośīkalā. Pāi-grāma is retained as a quiet waypoint between such memories, part of the sacred geography that pilgrims traverse on the outer round. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Pinthānā
summary: Village on the outer Vraja circuit between Pāi-grāma and Śṛṅgāra in the traditional list.
body: Pinthānā is remembered here as village on the outer Vraja circuit between Pāi-grāma and Śṛṅgāra in the traditional list. Pinthānā is set down in the Bhauma Vṛndāvana route between Pāi-grāma and Śṛṅgāra, with Sondha, Vanacārī, Khambi and Hāsanapura following farther along the same arc. No distinct pastime is given for the village, and it is the circuit itself that gives the name its place in devotion. Walking this outer path, pilgrims move from the meal memories of Bhojana-thālī toward the confidential gardens of the southern petal. Sondha farther on recalls Sannanda, Nanda's younger brother and trusted counsellor, while Hāsanapura belongs to the forest of humour where the gopas' laughter still seems to echo. Pinthānā is honoured as one of the names encountered between such places, a reminder that the whole landscape of Vraja, not only its famous groves and lakes, is treated as a field of Kṛṣṇa's presence. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Sondha
summary: Residence of Sannanda, Nanda Mahārāja's wise brother, whose counsel guided Vraja's move to Vṛndāvana and Govardhana worship.
body: Sondha is remembered here as residence of Sannanda, Nanda Mahārāja's wise brother, whose counsel guided Vraja's move to Vṛndāvana and Govardhana worship. Sondha lies just east of Cāmelivana and is remembered as the home of Sannanda, also called Sunanda, Nanda Mahārāja's younger brother and a trusted adviser to the cowherd king. The pilgrimage lists place it on the outer circuit between Śṛṅgāra and Vanacārī, so pilgrims reach it as they approach Vṛndāvana's southern border. Tradition recalls Sannanda's steady wisdom at two turning points. After Yaśodā bound Kṛṣṇa and the yamala-arjuna trees fell, he urged Nanda to leave Mahāvana for the safer, grass-rich forests of Vṛndāvana. Years later he supported Kṛṣṇa's request that the family honour Govardhana, the cows and the brāhmaṇas instead of Indra, explaining that the worship Kṛṣṇa proposed would also fulfil Indra's purpose. Sannanda established his household beside Cāmelivana, and the town took his name. Devotees remember him as gentle and generous, a master of buffalo herds who pleased Kṛṣṇa with yogurt dishes and served Him with unwavering devotion. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja, Arjuna, Indra. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Khambī (Khambi)
summary: Boundary hillock where Balarāma set a pillar marking Vṛndāvana's edge and warning devotees to keep Kṛṣṇa's shelter.
body: Khambī (Khambi) is remembered here as boundary hillock where Balarāma set a pillar marking Vṛndāvana's edge and warning devotees to keep Kṛṣṇa's shelter. South of Vanacārī, Khāmbī is a low hill where the cowherd boys played while their cattle grazed on the grass below. Tradition identifies it as the edge of Vṛndāvana: Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma told Their friends that beyond this point the modes of nature hold sway, while within it the land retains its Vaikuṇṭha character. Balarāma traced a line along the summit to show the limit. The boys, though never truly under material influence, tested the warning in play, stepping across and darting back before boasting at lunch of their boldness. Out of compassion for them and for future visitors, Balarāma cut a great pillar from the hillside with His plough and set it on the peak as a lasting marker. Devotees honour that pillar as a solemn reminder to remain within the shelter of Vṛndāvana and never turn from Kṛṣṇa in search of ordinary enjoyment. The name marks this as a hill sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Hāsanapura
summary: Holy town in Hāsyavana where Kṛṣṇa's laughter with the cowherd boys became the mellow of divine humour.
body: Hāsanapura is remembered here as holy town in Hāsyavana where Kṛṣṇa's laughter with the cowherd boys became the mellow of divine humour. Hāsanapura stands within Hāsyavana, the wooded tip of Vraja's southern petal, and is honoured as the capital of the secondary mellow of humour. Tradition says that pure chanters may still catch the gopas' laughter echoing among the trees, and that the sound itself brings on smiles and mirth. Once the boys sat in a ring beneath a large tree at lunchtime, and Kṛṣṇa appeared to be seated beside every one of them. They teased Him about His infant victories over Pūtanā and Tṛṇāvarta and over Aghāsura, joking that He must have a secret demon-slaying mantra or an amulet from Yaśodā. Smiling, Kṛṣṇa recalled Garga Muni's words at His naming ceremony and told them that He is the Supreme Lord who has become a gopa out of love. The boys' delight deepened into laughter that seemed to spread through birds, creepers and even insects, so the place remains saturated with that joyful exchange. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Mārava-grāma (Mārava)
summary: Yamunā-bank āśrama of Mārkaṇḍeya Ṛṣi, who after ages of austerity settled here to worship Kṛṣṇa.
body: Mārava-grāma (Mārava) is remembered here as yamunā-bank āśrama of Mārkaṇḍeya Ṛṣi, who after ages of austerity settled here to worship Kṛṣṇa. Mārava-grāma, also called Mārava, is identified as Mārkaṇḍeya Ṛṣi's āśrama on the Yamunā in the original Vraja; in New Vraja-dhāma the river is not visible here. The pilgrimage list sets it after Māhali, on the southern stretch of the outer circuit. The sage is remembered for almost unimaginable patience. Born in an earlier day of Brahmā, he kept a lifelong vow and served the Lord through sacrificial fire, the sun, his guru, brāhmaṇas and the Supersoul for six successive ages of Manu. When Nara-Nārāyaṇa appeared, Mārkaṇḍeya asked to witness material nature at work and was shown a cosmic flood, a banyan leaf and a divine infant who drew him within and revealed the universes. After further ages, and by Lord Śiva's grace, he realised Kṛṣṇa's supreme divinity. He then settled here to perform bhajana under Vṛndāvana's protection, and is said still to dwell on a hill in Mārava, absorbed in pure devotion. The name marks this as a hill sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Jedapura
summary: Named stop on the Bhauma Vraja circuit between Mārava and Bājanā, honoured within Vraja's sacred southern borderland.
body: Jedapura is remembered here as named stop on the Bhauma Vraja circuit between Mārava and Bājanā, honoured within Vraja's sacred southern borderland. Jedapura appears in the traditional Bhauma Vraja route immediately after Mārava and before Bājanā. The circuit belongs to the eighty-four-krośa parikrama, which begins and ends at Viśrāma-ghāṭa and encircles the whole holy dhāma. No individual episode is attached to this village in Vraja tradition. Its holiness is geographic rather than narrative: it stands within the precincts of Vraja, traversed after Mārava, where Mārkaṇḍeya Ṛṣi's old āśrama is remembered, and near Hāsanapura with its wood of laughter. Tradition notes that some parts of Vraja are not linked with a specific pastime of the Lord, yet because they lie inside His eternal realm they still deserve respect. Devotees therefore keep Jedapura as a named waypoint, walking through it in remembrance of Kṛṣṇa's cowherd life and the sacred land that supports those pastimes. Its name, repeated in the pilgrimage list, helps hold the southern sector of the route together in the pilgrim's mind. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Bājanā
summary: Village named between Jedapura and Salākā on the outer Vraja parikrama, kept as a holy waypoint.
body: Bājanā is remembered here as village named between Jedapura and Salākā on the outer Vraja parikrama, kept as a holy waypoint. Bājanā is one of the successive village names recorded for the Bhauma Vraja circumambulation, coming after Jedapura and before Salākā. The route continues through the southern villages before turning back toward Vāndī and Baladeva. Vraja tradition does not recount a distinct līlā for this particular stop. Instead, it presents the village as part of a continuous chain of sacred place-names: each halt is honoured because it belongs to the land where Kṛṣṇa walked, herded cows and played with the gopas. Pilgrims who follow the outer path thus remember more than individual stories; they regard the entire field of Vraja as sanctified by the Lord's presence. Bājanā, though mentioned only by name, shares in that sanctity, and its place in the list preserves it for devotees who walk the circuit in faith. Even a quiet hamlet has a place in the garland of Vraja's pastime places. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. title: Salākā

Salākā is listed on the Bhauma Vraja parikrama between Bājanā and Pitorā, in the long southern segment that eventually returns toward Vāndī and the twelve-forest route. No separate story is told about the place. Its significance lies in being named within the circumference of the dhāma. Tradition explains that certain areas of Vraja have no specific pastime attached to them and are less widely known, yet they remain within the Lord's eternal abode and therefore merit honour. Devotees walking the circuit carry such names in meditation along with the better-known forests and lakes. Salākā thus serves as a reminder that Vraja is holy as a whole, not only at its celebrated sites, and that every village on the path can awaken remembrance of Kṛṣṇa's cowherd pastimes. body: Pitorā is remembered here as southern Vraja village on the outer circuit, named after Salākā and before Ṭetī-grāma in the pilgrimage list. Pitorā is one of the village names that follow one another in the traditional list of Bhauma Vraja stops. title: Ṭetī-grāma

Ṭetī-grāma appears in the Bhauma Vraja list of holy places on the outer circumambulation. It sits between Pitorā and Jāravā, part of the chain of settlements that carries the pilgrim onward toward Rāya and Kārabha. No detailed pastime is told about this village. Traditional principle, however, is clear: places not distinguished by a particular līlā are still inside Vraja's precincts and deserve the respect due to the Lord's own realm. Devotees therefore regard Ṭetī-grāma as one of the many names to be remembered while walking the circuit. Keeping it in the route preserves the fullness of the sacred map, in which Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma's presence is honoured across fields, groves and villages alike. The act of circumambulation turns each successive halt into an occasion for remembrance. The name marks this as a village sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Jāravā
summary: Jāravā is a named halt between Ṭetī-grāma and Rāya on the outer Vraja pilgrimage route.
body: Jāravā is a named halt between Ṭetī-grāma and Rāya on the outer Vraja pilgrimage route. Jāravā is honoured after Ṭetī-grāma and before Rāya. It belongs to the Bhauma Vraja section of the eighty-four-krośa parikrama, the circumambulation that honours the entire holy dhāma rather than a single forest. No standalone narrative is given for it. The reason for preserving the name is geographical and devotional: the village lies within the circuit of Vraja, the land where the Lord's childhood and cowherd pastimes were enacted. Pilgrims who repeat such names in order are reminded that the whole region, including its lesser-known settlements, is pervaded by Kṛṣṇa's presence. Jāravā thus takes its place among the many villages that devotees remember with respect as they complete the sacred round. The list continues onward through Kārabha to Vāndī and Baladeva, so the name belongs to the closing section of the long southern circuit. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Rāya
summary: Small place listed after Jāravā and before Kārabha among the outer Vraja parikrama stops.
body: Rāya is remembered here as small place listed after Jāravā and before Kārabha among the outer Vraja parikrama stops. Rāya is named in the Bhauma Vraja route between Jāravā and Kārabha, near the end of the southern sequence of villages before the route returns to Vāndī and Baladeva. Its holiness is derived from inclusion in the sacred circuit: the eighty-four-krośa path goes around the land made auspicious by Kṛṣṇa's descent to Vraja and by His life with Nanda's household. Keeping Rāya in the list allows devotees to remember even the smaller settlements as part of the Lord's domain. Meditating on them in order, pilgrims acknowledge that Vraja's sanctity extends beyond famous groves and kuṇḍas into the everyday villages of the cowherds. The name therefore functions as a call to remembrance along the path. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. title: Kārabha
summary: Village at the close of the southern Bhauma Vraja list, named after Rāya and before Vāndī.
body: Kārabha is remembered here as village at the close of the southern Bhauma Vraja list, named after Rāya and before Vāndī. Kārabha appears after Rāya and before Vāndī in the traditional list of Bhauma Vraja places. With that mention the southern arc of the outer journey bends back toward the better-known pastures associated with Balarāma. Tradition gives no separate account of a pastime here. Like other quiet names in the route, Kārabha is honoured simply by belonging to the precincts of Vraja, where the soil, cattle and cowherd households are all connected with Kṛṣṇa's manifest life. For pilgrims, reciting and visiting such places completes the circle of remembrance. The village stands as part of the sacred geography that devotees traverse in faith, acknowledging the Lord's presence not only in celebrated līlā sites but throughout the land He chose for His pastimes. The names that follow, Vāndī and Baladeva, lead the pilgrim onward from this closing village of the southern list. Figures linked with this place include Balarāma. title: Bali-ṭīlā
summary: Mound inland from Sūrya-ghāṭa where Bali Mahārāja's sacrifice and surrender to Vāmana are remembered.
body: Bali-ṭīlā is remembered here as mound inland from Sūrya-ghāṭa where Bali Mahārāja's sacrifice and surrender to Vāmana are remembered. Bali-ṭīlā is a raised mound set back from Sūrya-ghāṭa. Tradition remembers it as the site of Bali Mahārāja's Viśvajit sacrifice, undertaken to win mastery over the universes; the ground is described as darkened by ashes and rich with ghee from the offerings. That arena is where the demon king is said to have received weapons for his campaign against the demigods. The nearness of Sūrya-tīrtha deepens the association, for it was there that Bali pleased the sun god and received a cintāmaṇi gem and the power to conquer the worlds. Devotees come to the mound to pray to Lord Vāmana and to His devoted king for the gift of unconditional surrender. Bali's story is heard here as a lesson that ambition ends in dependence on the Lord, and that surrender, not conquest, opens the way to pure service. The name marks this as a sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. title: Sītā-Rāma
summary: Garden where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, at the gopīs' request, entered the roles of Sītā and Rāma in exile.
body: Sītā-Rāma is remembered here as garden where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, at the gopīs' request, entered the roles of Sītā and Rāma in exile. Sītā-Rāma is a garden on the eastern petal, close to the outer parikrama path. The gopīs, whose boys often acted out the Rāmāyaṇa, asked the divine couple to reveal Themselves in the roles of Rāma and Sītā during exile. In a cottage-like grove resembling Pañcavaṭī, they dressed Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in simple ascetic clothes, made flower ornaments and placed a blossom bow and quiver beside Kṛṣṇa. As the girls sang of Agastya Muni, the Godāvarī and Lakṣmaṇa's cottage, the couple became wholly absorbed in rāma-līlā; even Śyāma's hue is said to have turned green. The gopīs later concluded that the grove had truly become Pañcavaṭī. The cottage where the couple adorned Themselves as forest exiles remains the focus of devotion, allowing visitors to enter this rare pastime in which Kṛṣṇa's Vraja identity and Lord Rāma's exile meet. It lies on a parikrama route used to move through the sacred landscape. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Nīgānyā
summary: Forest halt where the gopīs stopped Kṛṣṇa and challenged His detour during their pilgrimage to Kośīkalā.
body: Nīgānyā is remembered here as forest halt where the gopīs stopped Kṛṣṇa and challenged His detour during their pilgrimage to Kośīkalā. Nīgānyā, east of Vichora, recalls a pilgrimage the gopīs made from Yāvaṭā to Kośīkalā to bathe in Gomatī-kuṇḍa. Kṛṣṇa met them near Sevā-kuñja, claimed He was going to the same holy city and persuaded them to take a quiet forest path rather than the village road. He then lengthened the journey with a detour through Patharālī and Parehī, carrying their worship articles and praising their beauty as He went. At Nīgānyā the suspicious girls finally halted Him, and Rādhā pointed out that the supposed shortcut had become the long way. When His denials turned to playful evasions, the gopīs laughed and repeated His words, and the place took its name from that teasing cross-examination. The site preserves the affection of companions who knew Kṛṣṇa's ways yet delighted in catching Him out. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Agravana
summary: Remote forest where Caitanya Mahāprabhu first entered Vraja, filled with ecstasy and older ṛṣi tīrthas.
body: Agravana is remembered here as remote forest where Caitanya Mahāprabhu first entered Vraja, filled with ecstasy and older ṛṣi tīrthas. Agravana lies beyond Bodhi-tīrtha in a remote part of the dhāma. Tradition remembers it as the forest where Caitanya Mahāprabhu first came into Vraja from Prayāga: overwhelmed with love, He rolled on the ground, embraced the trees and urged the animals to chant Kṛṣṇa's name. Devotees recall that the cows followed Him, deer licked Him, trees and vines offered fruit, while two parrots competing to praise Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa gladdened Him as He rested. The place is therefore alive with the memory of ecstatic saṅkīrtana. Agravana also holds older tīrthas: Reṇukā-āśrama, Paraśurāma's birthplace, a sacrifice ground used against the wicked, and a yajña-śālā linked to Bharata Mahārāja's offering of seven spotted deer. These sacred traces join the history of Vraja's ṛṣis to Caitanya's own arrival. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Surabhivana
summary: Expansive Govardhana forest where Surabhi and Indra bathed Kṛṣṇa, creating Govinda-kuṇḍa and acclaiming Him king of the cows.
body: Surabhivana is remembered here as expansive Govardhana forest where Surabhi and Indra bathed Kṛṣṇa, creating Govinda-kuṇḍa and acclaiming Him king of the cows. Surabhivana is a wide, welcoming forest on the Govardhana circuit, reaching from Gaurī-tīrtha as far as Govinda-kuṇḍa. The pilgrim keeps it to the right while circumambulating Girirāja, and its groves of fruit and flowers have long been associated with the hill's hidden sweetness. The central tradition is the ceremonial bath: Surabhi, the wish-fulfilling cow, and Indra bathed Kṛṣṇa here with celestial water. The water gathered as Govinda-kuṇḍa, where His lordship over the cows was proclaimed, and Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī's verses still invoke that coronation. Because the lake is tucked behind Girirāja's peacock form, Vasudeva chose this area for Bhāguri Muni's protective sacrifice, and Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa could sport here unseen. Mādhavendra Purī's bhajana-kuṭīra nearby adds a later layer of devotion to the same sacred wood. Figures linked with this place include Indra. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Premavana
summary: Love-saturated wood around Prema-sarovara, where the lake's waters feed its trees and a rāsa platform is honoured.
body: Premavana is remembered here as love-saturated wood around Prema-sarovara, where the lake's waters feed its trees and a rāsa platform is honoured. Premavana lies at the western corner where the pilgrimage path meets the road between Nandagrāma and Varṣāṇā. Its name describes its mood: the forest is steeped in the rare, confidential love whose liquid form fills Prema-sarovara at its heart. The lake is octagonal, and its waters are said to have permeated the cintāmaṇi soil, nourishing the grasses, creepers and trees with the highest shade of prema. On its bank stand a temple of Prema-bihārī, a platform marking the rāsa dance and a swing where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are said to sport. The wood also remembers lighter exchanges, such as the bumblebee that mistook Rādhā's face for a lotus while Madhumaṅgala dozed as doorkeeper. Devotees honour both the secluded groves and the lake, treating the whole setting as a woodland counterpart of Prema-sarovara. The name marks this as a temple site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Candra-kūpa
summary: One of Vraja's ten sacred wells, listed beside Candra-sarovara, the lake of Kṛṣṇa's moonlit rāsa dance.
body: Candra-kūpa is remembered here as one of Vraja's ten sacred wells, listed beside Candra-sarovara, the lake of Kṛṣṇa's moonlit rāsa dance. Candra-kūpa appears in the traditional list of the ten wells of Vraja, where it is paired with Candra-sarovara. Tradition gives the well no independent story, so it is honoured as part of the network of holy waters that belonged to the cowherd settlements. The associated lake is rich in memory. Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs rested on its bank before a spring rāsa dance, and the moon god is said to have hung motionless overhead, shedding tears of ecstasy into the water; hence the name Candra-sarovara. The lake is described as octagonal, with a resting place called Śṛṅgāra-mandira and a shrine of Rādhā-Candrabihārī, and Sūradāsa's samādhi is nearby. Devotees who remember the well also remember these surroundings, in which water, moonlight and love meet. The name marks this as a temple site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Bhāṇḍīra-kūpa
summary: Sacred well in Bhāṇḍīravana, the Yamunā-side grove of Kṛṣṇa's wrestling, fire-swallowing and Balarāma's victory.
body: Bhāṇḍīra-kūpa is remembered here as sacred well in Bhāṇḍīravana, the Yamunā-side grove of Kṛṣṇa's wrestling, fire-swallowing and Balarāma's victory. Bhāṇḍīra-kūpa is listed among the ten wells of Vraja and located in Bhāṇḍīravana, the Yamunā-side forest of the famous banyan. The appendix does not tell a separate tale about the well itself; its sanctity comes from the pastimes of the grove around it. Under the Bhāṇḍīraka tree Kṛṣṇa wrestled with the cowherd boys and with Rādhā and the gopīs, swallowed a ring of fire meant to destroy Vraja, and saw Balarāma dispose of Pralamba. Tradition calls the tree a jewel among the pastime places adorning the riverbank. Devotees also recall Kṛṣṇa embracing that tree and playing from its roots a melody meant to draw Rādhā's heart. Remembering these events while honouring the well keeps the whole grove present to the mind. The water and the shade belong to one sacred landscape of play, danger and divine protection. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. This description remains a draft and can be deepened after review.

title: Karaṇavedha-kūpa
summary: Sacred well at Gokula, Nanda Mahārāja's early home, listed among Vraja's ten holy wells without a separate legend.
body: Karaṇavedha-kūpa is remembered here as sacred well at Gokula, Nanda Mahārāja's early home, listed among Vraja's ten holy wells without a separate legend. Karaṇavedha-kūpa is one of the ten wells named in the appendix of Vraja's sacred waters. The list places it at Gokula, the early settlement of Nanda Mahārāja, before Kṛṣṇa's family established themselves at Nandagrāma. No distinct episode is told about this particular well. It is remembered instead within the group of kūpas connected with the cowherd world — Nanda-kūpa, Indra-kūpa, Kṛṣṇa-kūpa and others — each of which served the daily life of the Vraja-vāsīs and is honoured for that association. Gokula itself is saturated with the memory of Kṛṣṇa's earliest years among the cows and His parents' household. Devotees who recall Karaṇavedha-kūpa therefore think of that humble setting, where the ordinary necessities of cattle and family were gathered into the sacred geography of the dhāma. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja, Indra. The name marks this as a village sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Advaita-vaṭa
summary: Advaita-vaṭa is a banyan tree in the small forest of Kiśoravana, beside a cottage, and it is a pratibhū representative of the tree of the same name in Bhauma Vṛndāvana.
body: Advaita-vaṭa is a banyan tree in the small forest of Kiśoravana, beside a cottage, and it is a pratibhū representative of the tree of the same name in Bhauma Vṛndāvana. Advaita Ācārya stayed in a residence below this tree during His visits to Vṛndāvana, where He saw the beauty of Sevā-kuñja. He later discovered Madana-gopāla buried under the earth of Dvādaśāditya-ṭīlā and worshipped the Deity at this spot. Before leaving for Bengal, He entrusted the Deity to the brāhmaṇa Dāmodara Chaube in Mathurā for safekeeping. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. Advaita-vaṭa is preserved here chiefly through its name and setting. Advaita-vaṭa belongs to the wider set of Vraja sites held in remembrance. title: Aghavana
summary: Aghavana is the forest in Bhauma Vṛndāvana where Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Aghāsura, and a place of the same name in New Vraja-dhāma commemorates that pastime.
body: Aghavana is the forest in Bhauma Vṛndāvana where Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Aghāsura, and a place of the same name in New Vraja-dhāma commemorates that pastime. The killing happened before Brahmā's bewilderment and was reported to the Vraja-vāsīs a year later. The demigods glorified Kṛṣṇa's victory at Jayeta to the north, and the cowherd boys then ate lunch together at Jonai. The place is also called Sāpaulī or Sarpasthalī, as Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī refers to it. The name marks this as a wooded sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. title: Airāvata-kuṇḍa
summary: Airāvata-kuṇḍa is a lake in Surabhivana that was filled with Gaṅgā water brought by Indra's elephant Airāvata for bathing Kṛṣṇa.
body: Airāvata-kuṇḍa is a lake in Surabhivana that was filled with Gaṅgā water brought by Indra's elephant Airāvata for bathing Kṛṣṇa. The dust of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet mixes with its water and makes it more potent, and the dust of pure devotees' feet purifies it even more. The nearby Govinda-kuṇḍa was formed from the water used to bathe Kṛṣṇa in the same forest, where Surabhi and Indra performed the bathing. An appendix describes how the dust of devotees' feet purifies sacred waters. Figures linked with this place include Indra. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region.
