title: Aiṁṭhā-kadamba
summary: Aiṁṭhā-kadamba is a kadamba tree in Paīṭhā, near Nārāyaṇa-sarovara, the lake where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa finally met after separation.
body: Aiṁṭhā-kadamba is a kadamba tree in Paīṭhā, near Nārāyaṇa-sarovara, the lake where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa finally met after separation. Kṛṣṇa twisted this tree into a circle to reassure His friends. The predominant mood of Paīṭhā is separation from Kṛṣṇa, because Rādhārāṇī's feelings of separation were responsible for her success. Tradition describes the kadamba trees of Vṛndāvana as desire trees that take part in Kṛṣṇa's pastimes. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. Groves, paths and local landmarks give the site its setting. title: Akrūra-kuṇḍa
summary: Akrūra-kuṇḍa, also called Akrūra-tīrtha, lies at the far end of Kadambavana in New Vraja-dhāma and is not the Yamunā ghāṭa at the border of Mathurā.
body: Akrūra-kuṇḍa, also called Akrūra-tīrtha, lies at the far end of Kadambavana in New Vraja-dhāma and is not the Yamunā ghāṭa at the border of Mathurā. Here Akrūra dismounted his chariot, embraced Kṛṣṇa's footprints in the dust of Nandagrāma, and first saw his nephews Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. This visit was part of Kaṁsa's plan to lure the divine brothers to Mathurā and kill them. Caitanya Mahāprabhu also jumped into the waters of Akrūra-kuṇḍa, overwhelmed by love for Kṛṣṇa. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. Its place in the circuit is kept alongside related sacred spots in the same region. The nearby Yamunā ties this spot to other sacred places along the river. title: Akrūra-tīrtha
summary: Akrūra-tīrtha is a ghāṭa on the Yamunā at the entrance to Mathurā, where Akrūra stopped to bathe while driving Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma along a circuitous route.
body: Akrūra-tīrtha is a ghāṭa on the Yamunā at the entrance to Mathurā, where Akrūra stopped to bathe while driving Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma along a circuitous route. Kṛṣṇa unyoked the bulls there and arranged the carts into an encampment before going into the city with Balarāma. Between Murāra and Akrūra-tīrtha lie Motī and Khapāna, where Kṛṣṇa once garlanded Rādhārāṇī with a necklace of pearls. Tradition tells of Caitanya Mahāprabhu's reaction when people reported a miracle of Kṛṣṇa dancing on Kāliya's hoods at Akrūra-tīrtha. Figures linked with this place include Caitanya Mahāprabhu. title: Akṣaya-vaṭa
summary: Akṣaya-vaṭa is a banyan tree also known as Bhāṇḍīraka, and the forest around it is called Bhāṇḍīravana.
body: Akṣaya-vaṭa is a banyan tree also known as Bhāṇḍīraka, and the forest around it is called Bhāṇḍīravana. A pratibhū representative of this tree was designated in New Vraja-dhāma, which means the tree is commemorated along the parikrama path. Lord Balarāma killed Pralambāsura in one Bhāṇḍīravana, while Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were married in another. Bhāṇḍīravana is one of the twelve forests of Vraja. title: Belvana

body: Belvana is the same forest as Bilvavana and Śrīvana, and it lies at the edge of Māna-sarovara on the eighth forest of Vraja. Its name comes from the bilva, or bel, rose-apple trees growing there, and from the goddess of fortune, Śrī, who still performs austerities here to attain love like that of the gopīs. Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited this forest and recalled while resting here how Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd boys had played. body: Beḍokhora-kuñja is a garden surrounding the samādhi of Kavirāja Gosvāmī and is rich with the pastimes of the divine couple. The lake here is called Kuntala-kuṇḍa, since its waters served the hair of both Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. title: Bhānu-sarovara
summary: Bhānu-sarovara, also called Vṛṣabhānu-kuṇḍa, lies on the eastern border of Varṣāṇā, and Mahārāja Vṛṣabhānu bathes there each morning.
body: Bhānu-sarovara, also called Vṛṣabhānu-kuṇḍa, lies on the eastern border of Varṣāṇā, and Mahārāja Vṛṣabhānu bathes there each morning. Some authorities say Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī appeared in Rāval, while others say She appeared from a lotus in this lake, and tradition holds that both views are correct. Rādhā and Her gopī friends bathe on one side of the lake while Kṛṣṇa and His friends bathe on the other, and when only Rādhā and the gopīs are present Kṛṣṇa appears, and the divine couple play water games such as hide-and-seek among the lotuses. The Deities of Laṛilī-Lāl, first established by Vajranābha, once took shelter in the lake's waters when they were under threat. Kṛṣṇa once came to this tree alone and played a flute melody composed to attract Śrī Rādhā's heart, and He is also said to have wrestled with Rādhā and the gopīs beneath its boughs. Brahmā performed the wedding of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa beneath a banyan of this name, which Vraja tradition distinguishes from a second Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa across the Yamunā where Pralambāsura was killed. title: Bhūlanvana
summary: Bhūlanvana is a dense forest south of Koṭaravana, and its name is explained in two ways, either because many people lose their way there or because Kṛṣṇa warned His friend Subala not to forget (bhulāno) his promise to arrange a meeting with Rādhā.
body: Bhūlanvana is a dense forest south of Koṭaravana, and its name is explained in two ways, either because many people lose their way there or because Kṛṣṇa warned His friend Subala not to forget (bhulāno) his promise to arrange a meeting with Rādhā. Beneath a large bakula tree in the forest is Karamaṇa, where Kṛṣṇa searched for Rādhā late one evening, and in His separation He fainted on a bed of moss and did not meet Her that night. body: Cakra-tīrtha is a ghāṭa on the Mathurā riverfront beside Ambarīṣa-ṭīlā, where Kṛṣṇa's disc, which He gave to King Ambarīṣa, is said to reside. Uddhava met Kṛṣṇa near this place beneath a banyan tree by the Yamunā, having promised to bring Kṛṣṇa back home to Vraja. Sanātana Gosvāmī lived here, worshipping Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in a cottage facing Lord Śiva, and he left his body here. title: Devī-dhāma

body: Devī-dhāma is remembered as the mundane world, the lowest of the realms, above which lie Maheśa-dhāma and Hari-dhāma, and highest of all is Kṛṣṇa's own realm, Goloka. This verse glorifies Goloka Vṛndāvana as superior to all the Lord's other abodes. Tradition says that Vṛṣabhānu-pura, Varṣāṇā, is untouched by Hari-dhāma or Devī-dhāma, because it is permeated by Rādhā's sweet youthfulness. Figures linked with this place include Brahmā. title: Dhanus-tīrtha

body: Dhanus-tīrtha is the place of the sacrificial bow in Kṛṣṇa Valley, the open area in Mathurā flanked by two life-size resin elephants, and it lies beside Raṅga-bhūmi, the wrestling arena. Kṛṣṇa broke the bow here, and nearby Kaṁsa-ṭīlā marks where Kaṁsa was slain. Raṅgeśvara Mahādeva, whom Kaṁsa installed in the hope of defeating Kṛṣṇa, protects this corner of Mathurā, and the wrestling tournament took place on Śiva-rātri. title: Dharma-kuṇḍa
summary: Dharma-kuṇḍa is a secluded lake in Kāmyavana, full of lotuses and lilies, where the Pāṇḍavas came while thirsty during their stay in Kāman.
body: Dharma-kuṇḍa is a secluded lake in Kāmyavana, full of lotuses and lilies, where the Pāṇḍavas came while thirsty during their stay in Kāman. While they chased a deer that had run off with a brāhmaṇa's ladle and araṇi sticks, Nakula went to fetch water and died after ignoring a celestial warning, and Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhīma each went to the lake and died in the same way. The parikrama of Kāmyavana traditionally begins with a bath at Dharma-kuṇḍa or Vimala-kuṇḍa, and pilgrims often visit Dharma-kuṇḍa inside Kāman. title: Dhoyāni-kuṇḍa

body: Dhoyāni-kuṇḍa is remembered here as a small lake near the main road to Varṣāṇā, where Mother Yaśodā's servants washed the yogurt pots while singing of Kṛṣṇa. Vraja tradition describes Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa at its ghāṭa, glancing at each other as they absentmindedly dipped their pots, so enchanted by each other's youthful beauty that they dropped the pots or forgot to pull them out until the gopīs' laughter woke them. title: Dhruva-ghāṭa
summary: This is one of the twenty-four bathing ghāṭas of Mathurā, ninth in a traditional sequence.
body: Dhruva-ghāṭa is remembered here as this is one of the twenty-four bathing ghāṭas of Mathurā, ninth in a traditional sequence. Rūpa Gosvāmī, sent by Lord Caitanya to Vṛndāvana in 1517, lived here until Sanātana Gosvāmī joined him. In 1519 the two brothers met at Dhruva-ghāṭa and realised their long-cherished dream of living together in Vṛndāvana, after which Rūpa settled in Sevā-kuñja and Sanātana lived atop Dvādaśāditya-ṭīlā. title: Dhruva-tīrtha
summary: Downstream from Vaṭasvāmī-tīrtha, this is where child Dhruva performed severe austerities for four months, standing on one leg and concentrating fully on the Lord, and the pressure of his big toe left footprints that are still visible.

Devotees who want unwavering determination in devotional service bathe and worship here. Overlooking it is Nārada-ṭīlā, from which Nārada Muni watched Dhruva's obstinate determination, and nearby Saptarṣi-ghāṭa is the place where the seven sages are associated with the site. title: Dhyāna-kuṇḍa
summary: This lake marks the spot where Kṛṣṇa sat in meditation (dhyāna) on Rādhā, remembering Her features, Her witty talks, and their recent dancing and enjoyment in the groves.
body: Dhyāna-kuṇḍa is remembered here as this lake marks the spot where Kṛṣṇa sat in meditation (dhyāna) on Rādhā, remembering Her features, Her witty talks, and their recent dancing and enjoyment in the groves. Because His thoughts of Rādhā are not different from Her, they formed a pathway to Her lotus feet, and the lake where that pathway began is called Dhyāna-kuṇḍa. title: Dhārāpatana-tīrtha
summary: Located at the foot of Kaṁsa-ṭīlā, part of the fortification around Mathurā, its waters are said to assure heavenly happiness or, if desired, eternal life in Vaikuṇṭha.
body: Dhārāpatana-tīrtha is remembered here as located at the foot of Kaṁsa-ṭīlā, part of the fortification around Mathurā, its waters are said to assure heavenly happiness or, if desired, eternal life in Vaikuṇṭha. The immortal snake Ananta, who protects the dhāma from here, appeared to shelter Vasudeva and baby Kṛṣṇa from wind and rain on their way to Gokula. Tradition tells of a king and queen who, after the queen's previous life of drowning here, bathed at the next tīrtha, Saṁyamana-tīrtha, and went to Goloka. title: Dhīra-samīra-ghāṭa

body: Dhīra-samīra-ghāṭa is remembered here as on the shore between Keśī-ghāṭa and Vaṁśīvaṭa in New Vraja-dhāma, its gardens and groves represent the place where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa perfected Their youth. In Bhauma Vṛndāvana the gardens have disappeared and the Yamunā no longer flows nearby, yet the breezes (samīra) still blow softly (dhīra) there. title: Domīlavana

body: Domīlavana is remembered here as reached by following the parikrama path counterclockwise around Nandagrāma, this expansive forest is where the two lovers, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, meet, and its name is explained by dvā (two) and milana (meeting). summary: Also called Saṅkarṣaṇa-kuṇḍa and Kṣīra-sāgara, this lake is where the priests of the Deity Daujī threw Him upside down when soldiers of Muslim kings came to raze the temple.
body: Dugdha-kuṇḍa is remembered here as also called Saṅkarṣaṇa-kuṇḍa and Kṣīra-sāgara, this lake is where the priests of the Deity Daujī threw Him upside down when soldiers of Muslim kings came to raze the temple. The Deity remained in the lake for many years until cowherd men noticed two cows pouring their milk onto a protruding rock by the lakeside. title: Motī-kuṇḍa
summary: A lake near Nandagrāma that is the setting of a pearl pastime.

When the gopīs copied Him at Muktā-kuṇḍa near Varṣāṇā and failed, they had to bargain with Kṛṣṇa for pearls, and tradition says those negotiations can still be heard at Motī-kuṇḍa. title: Pāni-ghāṭa

body: Pāni-ghāṭa is the Yamunā landing where Rādhā led the gopīs, on Kṛṣṇa's advice, to ask the river to part on the strength of His brahmacarya vow. body: Pāpamocana-kuṇḍa lies to the east of Indra-dhvaja-tīrtha, and is famed, together with Ṛṇamocana-kuṇḍa to its west, for its sanctity, since devotees who bathe in them are freed from all vices. body: Rudra-kuṇḍa lies in the centre of the larger Harajī-kuṇḍa in Bhauma Vṛndāvana, named for the gopa Hara, who played ball with Kṛṣṇa nearby, and Vaiṣṇavas visit it to honour Lord Śiva as the best of devotees. Its deep, clear water made it a favourite of Kṛṣṇa, His cowherd friends, and the gopīs, and Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā bathed and swam there, though Kṛṣṇa once left Rādhā, a weak swimmer, in the middle of the lake. Its pastimes are remembered as sad, recounting how the gopīs' weeping overflowed the lake when they learned Kṛṣṇa had gone to the Yamunā, and how the Vraja-vāsīs wept on its shore when Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma passed on their way to Mathurā. body: Rādhāvana is the area north of Abhirāma Ṭhākura's samādhi, bounded by Gauravana and Aṭalavana and reaching the Yamunā up to Jagannātha-ghāṭa, and it is named after Rādhā, who is as fond of it as of Her lake. body: Rāja-ghāṭa is a landing at the centre of Papaḍavana on the Yamunā, where boats once ferried people across the river. Kṛṣṇa disguised Himself as a boatman here, and when Rādhārāṇī and Her friends, carrying milk products to relatives in Rāval and Gokula, threatened to report the lazy boatman to the king (rāja), Kṛṣṇa revealed His identity and immersed them in bliss, which is why the landing is so named. body: Rāsa-kuṇḍa is a lake at Rāsolī, near Raṅkolī, where Kṛṣṇa called the gopīs visiting their parents in Varṣāṇā with His flute and enjoyed rāsa dancing beneath a large banyan tree. body: Svānanda-sukhada-kuñja is remembered here as a lotus-shaped island grove at the centre of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, belonging to Anaṅga-mañjarī, the manifestation of Balarāma who serves Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the mellow of amorous love. title: Sābalā-grāma
summary: A village in the Kāmyavana area of Bhauma Vṛndāvana, toward which tradition walked through a peaceful stretch of land.
body: Sābalā-grāma is remembered here as a village in the Kāmyavana area of Bhauma Vṛndāvana, toward which tradition walked through a peaceful stretch of land. In Kṛṣṇa’s time the encroaching desert had dried up the lakes in this area, so trees grew only in the damp lakebeds. The cowherd boys found it difficult to water their cows or bathe when they passed this way. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Sāhasī-kuṇḍa
summary: A lake in a banyan forest facing Nandagrāma, also called Sārasi-kuṇḍa, further from the road than Leovaṭa-kuṇḍa.
body: Sāhasī-kuṇḍa is remembered here as a lake in a banyan forest facing Nandagrāma, also called Sārasi-kuṇḍa, further from the road than Leovaṭa-kuṇḍa. Its name comes from sāhasī, meaning determined, which reflects the determination of the young gopīs to bring Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa together even so close to His home. The gopīs once brought Rādhā here, where Kṛṣṇa was waiting, and seated the divine couple on a decorated swing while they sang of His heroic pastimes. Mother Yaśodā could hear their saṅkīrtana from Nanda-bhavana. Figures linked with this place include Nanda Mahārāja. The name marks this as a water sacred site within the sacred geography of Vraja. title: Sārasi-kuṇḍa
summary: Another name for Sāhasī-kuṇḍa, meaning Swan Lake.
body: Sārasi-kuṇḍa is remembered here as another name for Sāhasī-kuṇḍa, meaning Swan Lake. Mother Yaśodā, unable to see her boys who were playing around the lake, called Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma the swans (sārasa) of her life, one black and one white, and the boys then decided to call the lake Sārasi-kuṇḍa. Both names have been used ever since. Behind the grove of banyan trees lies a fertile field called Muktā-tīrtha, where Kṛṣṇa watered His cows at a clear lake in the centre. title: Sūrya-ghāṭa
summary: A bathing place on the Yamunā where the sun god, Sūrya-nārāyaṇa, performed austerities so that he might directly see and serve Kṛṣṇa, and where he was eventually given assurance that his desire would be fulfilled.

The sun god appeared in person to Sāmba, freeing him from leprosy and letting him ride on the chariot of the sun. Inland from this ghāṭa is Bali-ṭīlā, where Bali Mahārāja performed the Viśvajit sacrifice. Rādhā once also set out toward this ghāṭa to worship the sun god. title: Sūrya-tīrtha

body: Sūrya-tīrtha is remembered here as a bathing place in Mathurā that destroys all sin, where Bali Mahārāja long ago pleased the sun god and received a cintāmaṇi gem and blessings to conquer the universe. title: Tapovana
summary: A secluded forest valley among hills where Nara-Nārāyaṇa Ṛṣi performs austerities even today.
body: Tapovana is remembered here as a secluded forest valley among hills where Nara-Nārāyaṇa Ṛṣi performs austerities even today. When King Indra sent Cupid and beautiful damsels to disturb the Lord’s meditation, the Lord calmly and politely welcomed them, and Cupid and his companions trembled in fear. The gopīs performed their worship of Kātyāyanī here, and the place is named Tapovana for the severe austerities they performed, and the sun god warmed their cold bodies. title: Taḍāga-tīrtha
summary: A forest northeast of Pāvana-sarovara, where Parjanya Mahārāja, Kṛṣṇa’s grandfather, gave up eating and drinking on Nārada’s advice and performed penance to obtain a worthy descendant, until a voice from heaven promised five sons, the best of whom would be Nanda.
body: Taḍāga-tīrtha is remembered here as a forest northeast of Pāvana-sarovara, where Parjanya Mahārāja, Kṛṣṇa’s grandfather, gave up eating and drinking on Nārada’s advice and performed penance to obtain a worthy descendant, until a voice from heaven promised five sons, the best of whom would be Nanda. Sanātana Gosvāmī also performed bhajana here. title: Vajra-kuṇḍa
summary: A lake restored by Vajra after Kṛṣṇa left Vraja and the two lakes Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa had become simple ponds.
body: Vajra-kuṇḍa is remembered here as a lake restored by Vajra after Kṛṣṇa left Vraja and the two lakes Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa had become simple ponds. The lakes then became known as Kāñcana-kuṇḍa and Vajra-kuṇḍa. Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī later expanded Vajra-kuṇḍa into the present Śyāma-kuṇḍa, and the five sacred trees that were to be cut were allowed to remain after Mahārāja Yudhiṣṭhira appeared to him in a dream.
